name: Expose a Deployment: ClusterIP, headless, NodePort
objective: CKA › Services & Networking + Troubleshooting. Drill the whole pod-networking surface harder than the exam: how the CNI hands out pod IPs from the pod CIDR, the node-level CNI config, a no-hint diagnose-and-fix for a broken CNI, CoreDNS resolution, ClusterIP + endpoints, the full pod→Service datapath, headless Services, and NodePort. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: Expose a Deployment (kube-proxy wires the endpoints)
questions.teach:
A **ClusterIP** Service gets a stable virtual IP that **kube-proxy** load-balances to the backing pods. `kubectl expose deployment <d> --port=80` creates it and copies the Deployment's selector, so its Endpoints auto-populate with the pod IPs.

**Gotcha:** zero endpoints almost always means the selector doesn't match the pod labels — check `kubectl get endpoints <svc>`.
questions.prompt:
Deployment `web` (nginx, 3 replicas, label `app=web`) is already running in `cni-learn`. Expose it as a `ClusterIP` Service named `web` on port `80`.

Target: Service `web` is type ClusterIP, port 80, with 3 ready endpoint addresses.
questions.hint: `kubectl expose deployment web -n cni-learn --name=web --port=80`, then `kubectl get endpoints web -n cni-learn` (lists the pod IPs).
questions.solution:
kubectl expose deployment web -n cni-learn --name=web --port=80
kubectl get endpoints web -n cni-learn

verification.description: Service web: ClusterIP, port 80, 3 active endpoints

questions.eli5:
Imagine a pizza shop with three identical ovens (your pods) all baking the same pizza. Customers (other pods) don't want to memorize which oven is free, or care that ovens get swapped out when they break. They just want **one phone number** to call that always reaches *an* available oven.

A **ClusterIP Service** is that single phone number. `kubectl expose deployment web --port=80` creates it: Kubernetes picks a stable virtual IP, and the behind-the-scenes dispatcher (**kube-proxy**) forwards each call to one of the working ovens.

How does the Service know which ovens are "its" ovens? When you expose a Deployment, Kubernetes copies the Deployment's **selector** (the labels, like `app=web`) onto the Service. Any pod wearing those labels automatically gets added to a list called **Endpoints** — the real pod IPs the Service forwards to. Pods come and go; the Endpoints list updates itself.

So the flow is: one stable IP → kube-proxy → a live pod. The pods can be deleted, replaced, or scaled, and callers never notice.

**Watch out for:**

- **Zero endpoints = the number rings nowhere.** This almost always means the Service's selector doesn't match the pods' labels. Check with `kubectl get endpoints web` — empty means a label/selector mismatch.
- The Service's `port` is what callers dial; `targetPort` is the port the pod actually listens on. If you only set `port`, `targetPort` defaults to the same number.
- A pod must be **Ready** (passing its readiness probe) to appear in Endpoints. Not-ready pods are held out.
- ClusterIP is **cluster-internal only** — you can't reach it from your laptop without NodePort/LoadBalancer or a port-forward.
questions.deepDive:
## ClusterIP Services & Endpoints — full rundown

### The one-sentence model
A **Service** is a stable virtual IP + DNS name that **load-balances to a set of pods chosen by a label selector**. **kube-proxy** programs the datapath; the **EndpointSlice/Endpoints** objects hold the live pod IPs.

### Service types at a glance
| Type | Gets a clusterIP | Reachable from | Builds on |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ClusterIP** (default) | ✅ | inside the cluster only | — |
| **NodePort** | ✅ | `nodeIP:nodePort` from outside + clusterIP | ClusterIP |
| **LoadBalancer** | ✅ | external LB IP + NodePort + clusterIP | NodePort |
| **ExternalName** | ❌ | CNAME to an external DNS name | — |
| **Headless** (`clusterIP: None`) | ❌ (no VIP) | DNS returns pod IPs directly | — |

### Creating a ClusterIP Service
```bash
# expose copies the Deployment's selector automatically
kubectl expose deployment web --name=web --port=80

# expose with a different target port (pod listens on 8080)
kubectl expose deployment web --port=80 --target-port=8080

# imperative create (you supply the selector yourself)
kubectl create service clusterip web --tcp=80:80
```
Equivalent YAML:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  type: ClusterIP          # default; may be omitted
  selector:
    app: web               # must match the pods' labels
  ports:
  - port: 80               # the Service's virtual port
    targetPort: 80         # the container's port (defaults to port if omitted)
    protocol: TCP          # TCP (default) | UDP | SCTP
```

### port vs targetPort vs nodePort
| Field | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `port` | port on the Service's clusterIP | required |
| `targetPort` | port on the pod/container traffic is forwarded to | = `port` |
| `nodePort` | port opened on every node (NodePort/LoadBalancer only) | auto from 30000–32767 |

`targetPort` may be a **named port** (e.g. `targetPort: http`) that references `containerPort`'s `name` in the pod spec — handy when pods listen on different numeric ports.

### Endpoints / EndpointSlices
The Service controller watches pods matching the selector and writes their IP:port into:
- **Endpoints** (`v1`, legacy, one object per Service) — what `kubectl get endpoints` shows.
- **EndpointSlices** (`discovery.k8s.io/v1`, current, scales better) — `kubectl get endpointslices`.

```bash
kubectl get endpoints web                 # NAME  ENDPOINTS  (list of podIP:port)
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web
kubectl describe svc web                   # shows Selector + Endpoints together
```
Only **Ready** pods (passing readiness probes) are listed as serving endpoints; not-ready ones are held out so traffic isn't sent to them.

### How a request flows
1. Client resolves `web.<ns>.svc.cluster.local` → clusterIP (via CoreDNS).
2. Packet to `clusterIP:80` hits kube-proxy rules (iptables or IPVS).
3. kube-proxy **DNATs** to one endpoint pod IP:targetPort (random/round-robin).
4. CNI carries the packet pod→pod; the backend replies.

kube-proxy does **not** sit in the data path as a proxy process (for iptables/IPVS modes) — it only programs kernel rules. The clusterIP is virtual: it never answers ping and isn't bound to any interface.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Zero endpoints** → selector/label mismatch. Compare `kubectl get svc web -o wide` (Selector) with `kubectl get pods --show-labels`.
- **`expose` copies the Deployment's selector** — if you later change pod labels, the Service may go empty.
- Forgetting `--target-port` when the container listens on a non-80 port → connection refused even with endpoints present.
- clusterIP is **immutable** after creation; to change it you recreate the Service.
- A Service with **no selector** gets no auto-endpoints — you'd manage Endpoints/EndpointSlices manually (used for external backends).
- clusterIP is unreachable from outside the cluster; use NodePort/LoadBalancer or `kubectl port-forward` for external access.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl expose deployment web --name=web --port=80
kubectl get svc web -o wide          # TYPE=ClusterIP, SELECTOR
kubectl get endpoints web            # should list 3 podIP:80 pairs
kubectl describe svc web             # Selector + Endpoints in one view
```

questions.title: Pod-to-pod through the Service
questions.teach:
This exercises the full datapath at once: DNS resolves `web.cni-learn` to the clusterIP, kube-proxy DNATs it to a backend pod, and the CNI carries the packet so nginx replies. Fetch it with `wget -qO- http://web.cni-learn`.

**Gotcha:** busybox `wget` needs `-qO-` to print to stdout — without it you get a downloaded file and empty logs.
questions.prompt:
Run a pod named `client` (image `busybox:1.36`, `--restart=Never`) that fetches `http://web.cni-learn` and prints the response.

Target: `client`'s logs show the nginx welcome page (it reached the Service).
questions.hint: `kubectl run client -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never --command -- wget -qO- http://web.cni-learn`, then `kubectl logs client -n cni-learn`.
questions.solution:
kubectl run client -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never --command -- wget -qO- http://web.cni-learn
kubectl logs client -n cni-learn   # <title>Welcome to nginx!</title>

verification.description: client reached the web Service (full CNI + kube-proxy datapath)

questions.eli5:
This step is like placing a phone call and actually hearing someone pick up — it proves the whole chain works end to end, not just that the phone exists.

When your `client` pod runs `wget http://web.cni-learn`, a surprising number of things happen in a split second:

1. **DNS lookup:** `web.cni-learn` is a Service name. CoreDNS translates it into the Service's virtual IP (its clusterIP) — like looking up a name in a phone book to get the number.
2. **kube-proxy routing:** The packet aimed at that virtual IP gets quietly rewritten (DNAT) to point at one real nginx pod's IP. The virtual IP is just a stand-in; kube-proxy swaps in a live backend.
3. **CNI delivery:** The cluster's pod network (the CNI plugin) actually carries the packet from your client pod to that nginx pod, even if they're on different machines.
4. **nginx replies** with its welcome page, and the response travels all the way back.

If every link holds, `client`'s logs show `<title>Welcome to nginx!</title>`. One successful fetch confirms DNS, kube-proxy, and pod networking are all healthy.

**Watch out for:**

- **busybox `wget` needs `-qO-`.** Without it, `wget` *downloads a file* silently and prints nothing — your logs look empty and you think it failed when it actually worked. `-q` = quiet, `-O-` = write to stdout.
- Use `--restart=Never` so it's a one-shot pod (a bare Pod), not a Deployment that keeps restarting.
- If DNS fails you'll see `bad address` / `can't resolve`; if routing fails you'll see a **timeout**; if nginx has zero endpoints you'll get **connection refused**. The symptom tells you which link broke.
- You can use the **short name** `web.cni-learn` only because the client is in the same cluster and relies on the DNS search list; from another namespace use the full `web.cni-learn.svc.cluster.local`.
questions.deepDive:
## The full pod → Service datapath — full rundown

### The one-sentence model
A request from one pod to a Service name traverses **four subsystems**: **CoreDNS** (name → clusterIP), **kube-proxy** (clusterIP → pod IP via DNAT), the **CNI** (pod-to-pod packet delivery), and the **backend pod** (nginx replies). Testing it exercises all four at once.

### The four hops in detail
| Hop | Component | What it does | Failure symptom |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Resolve | CoreDNS | `web.cni-learn` → clusterIP (A record) | `bad address` / `can't resolve` |
| 2. Load-balance | kube-proxy | DNAT clusterIP:port → endpoint podIP:targetPort | connection **timeout** |
| 3. Deliver | CNI plugin | routes the packet pod→pod across nodes | timeout / no route |
| 4. Serve | backend pod | nginx returns 200 + HTML | `connection refused` (no/bad endpoint) |

### Running the test client
```bash
kubectl run client -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never \
  --command -- wget -qO- http://web.cni-learn
kubectl logs client -n cni-learn        # expect <title>Welcome to nginx!</title>
```
`--restart=Never` makes a bare **Pod** (not a Deployment) so it runs once and stops.

### busybox wget flags (exam-critical)
| Flag | Meaning | If omitted |
|---|---|---|
| `-q` | quiet (no progress noise) | noisy stderr |
| `-O-` | write body to **stdout** | wget **saves a file** `index.html`; logs look empty |
| `-T 5` | timeout 5s | hangs on a broken datapath |

> The classic trap: `wget http://web.cni-learn` *succeeds* but prints nothing because the body went to a file. Always `-qO-`.

### DNS names you can target
Service `web` in namespace `cni-learn`:
- `web` — only works from **inside the same namespace**
- `web.cni-learn` — works cluster-wide (relies on the `search` suffix)
- `web.cni-learn.svc.cluster.local` — the **fully-qualified** name, always unambiguous

### kube-proxy modes
| Mode | Mechanism | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **iptables** (default) | DNAT rules, random backend pick | O(n) rules; most clusters |
| **IPVS** | kernel LVS hashing | scales to many Services; needs modules loaded |
| **nftables** | newer nft rules | GA in recent versions |

In all modes kube-proxy only **programs kernel rules**; it is not an inline proxy process for ClusterIP traffic.

### Diagnosing a broken datapath
```bash
# DNS layer
kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- nslookup web.cni-learn
# endpoints present?
kubectl get endpoints web -n cni-learn
# is the clusterIP reachable / does nginx answer?
kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- wget -qO- -T5 http://web.cni-learn
# kube-proxy & CoreDNS health
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
kubectl get ds -n kube-system kube-proxy
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Empty log, exit 0** → you forgot `-O-`; wget saved a file.
- **Timeout** → kube-proxy rules missing (kube-proxy down) or CNI can't route — check `kubectl get ds -n kube-system kube-proxy` and pod IPs.
- **Connection refused** → Service has zero endpoints (selector mismatch or pods not Ready), or `targetPort` is wrong.
- **NXDOMAIN** → CoreDNS down, or you used a short name from the wrong namespace — use the FQDN.
- A `--restart=Never` pod stays `Completed`; re-running needs `kubectl delete pod client` first (or `--rm` with `-it`).

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl run client -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never \
  --command -- wget -qO- http://web.cni-learn
kubectl logs client -n cni-learn
# Welcome to nginx!  → DNS + kube-proxy + CNI + backend all healthy
```

questions.title: Headless Service returns pod IPs directly
questions.teach:
A **headless** Service (`clusterIP: None`) gets no virtual IP and no kube-proxy load-balancing. Instead its DNS name resolves straight to the **individual pod IPs** (A records), which is how StatefulSets address peers.

**Gotcha:** `clusterIP: None` must be set at create time; you can't flip an existing ClusterIP Service to headless by editing.
questions.prompt:
Create a **headless** Service named `web-hl` in `cni-learn` selecting `app=web` on port `80` (set `clusterIP: None`). It targets the existing `web` pods.

Target: Service `web-hl` has `clusterIP: None`, selector `app=web`, port 80, and endpoint addresses.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n cni-learn create service clusterip web-hl --clusterip=None --tcp=80:80`, then add the selector: `kubectl -n cni-learn set selector svc web-hl 'app=web'` (or write YAML with `clusterIP: None`).
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: web-hl, namespace: cni-learn }
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector: { app: web }
  ports: [ { port: 80, targetPort: 80 } ]
YAML
kubectl get endpoints web-hl -n cni-learn

verification.description: web-hl: clusterIP None, selector app=web, port 80, has endpoints

questions.eli5:
A normal ClusterIP Service is like a company's **main switchboard number**: you call one number and the switchboard forwards you to whichever employee is free. You never learn the employees' direct lines.

A **headless Service** throws away the switchboard. Instead of one number, when you look up the name you get back the **direct extensions of every employee** — the actual pod IPs, one DNS record each. There's no virtual IP and no kube-proxy forwarding; DNS hands you the real pods directly.

You make a Service headless by setting `clusterIP: None`. Then asking DNS for `web-hl.cni-learn` returns an A record **per pod**, so the caller can see and reach each individual pod.

Why would you want that? Because some apps — especially **StatefulSets** like databases — need to talk to *specific* peers by name (replica-0, replica-1, …), not a random one behind a load balancer. A headless Service is how pods discover each other as individuals.

**Watch out for:**

- **`clusterIP: None` must be set when you create the Service.** You cannot edit a normal ClusterIP Service into a headless one afterward — clusterIP is immutable. Delete and recreate.
- It still needs a **selector** so it knows which pods to list; without one you get no addresses.
- There's **no load balancing** — the client picks which returned IP to hit. If one pod is down, DNS may still have returned it.
- `kubectl get svc` shows `CLUSTER-IP` as `None` (that's correct, not a bug).
- The pods should be **Ready** to show up as normal A records; not-ready pods are listed separately (and only if `publishNotReadyAddresses` is set).
questions.deepDive:
## Headless Services — full rundown

### The one-sentence model
A **headless** Service (`clusterIP: None`) has **no virtual IP and no kube-proxy load-balancing**. Its DNS name resolves straight to the **individual pod IPs** (one A/AAAA record each), so clients address pods directly. It's the discovery mechanism behind StatefulSets.

### ClusterIP vs Headless
| Aspect | Normal ClusterIP | Headless (`clusterIP: None`) |
|---|---|---|
| Virtual IP | ✅ one stable VIP | ❌ none (`CLUSTER-IP = None`) |
| kube-proxy rules | ✅ DNAT/load-balance | ❌ not programmed |
| DNS `A` record | 1 record → clusterIP | N records → each pod IP |
| Load balancing | yes (kube-proxy) | no (client chooses) |
| Per-pod DNS | no | yes (with a governing StatefulSet) |
| Typical use | stateless fan-out | StatefulSet peer discovery, custom LB |

### Creating a headless Service
YAML (most reliable — set `clusterIP: None` at create time):
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-hl
  namespace: cni-learn
spec:
  clusterIP: None          # THIS makes it headless
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
```
Imperative:
```bash
kubectl create service clusterip web-hl --clusterip=None --tcp=80:80
kubectl set selector svc web-hl 'app=web'    # create service clusterip adds no selector
```

### DNS behaviour
```bash
# headless: returns one A record PER ready pod
nslookup web-hl.cni-learn.svc.cluster.local
#   Address: 10.244.1.5
#   Address: 10.244.2.7
#   Address: 10.244.1.9

# normal ClusterIP: returns the single VIP
nslookup web.cni-learn.svc.cluster.local
#   Address: 10.96.0.42
```

### StatefulSet peer names (why headless exists)
With a StatefulSet named `db` using `serviceName: web-hl`, each pod gets a **stable per-pod DNS name**:
```
<pod>.<service>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local
db-0.web-hl.cni-learn.svc.cluster.local
db-1.web-hl.cni-learn.svc.cluster.local
```
This lets replicas find each other by ordinal — essential for primary/replica databases, quorum systems, etc.

### Endpoints
A headless Service still populates **Endpoints/EndpointSlices** from its selector:
```bash
kubectl get endpoints web-hl -n cni-learn      # lists the pod IPs
```
By default only **Ready** pods are published. Set `spec.publishNotReadyAddresses: true` to include not-ready pods (StatefulSets often want this during startup).

### Headless with no selector
A headless Service **without a selector** returns whatever you put in its EndpointSlices manually, or (for `ExternalName`-style) CNAMEs — used to front external hosts with a stable in-cluster name.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`clusterIP: None` is immutable** — you cannot `kubectl edit` a ClusterIP Service into headless (or vice versa). Delete and recreate.
- `kubectl create service clusterip --clusterip=None` creates it **without a selector**; you must add one (`kubectl set selector`) or it resolves to nothing.
- **No load balancing** — the client picks an IP; a down pod may still be in the returned set until it goes not-ready.
- `CLUSTER-IP = None` in `kubectl get svc` is expected, not an error.
- Per-pod DNS names only exist when a **StatefulSet** governs the pods via `serviceName`; bare pods/Deployments get only the set of A records, not stable per-pod hostnames.

### Quick reference
```yaml
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector: { app: web }
  ports: [ { port: 80, targetPort: 80 } ]
```
```bash
kubectl get svc web-hl -n cni-learn            # CLUSTER-IP: None
kubectl get endpoints web-hl -n cni-learn      # pod IPs listed
nslookup web-hl.cni-learn.svc.cluster.local    # one A record per pod
```

questions.title: NodePort opens the Service on every node
questions.teach:
A **NodePort** Service builds on ClusterIP and also opens a port (default range `30000–32767`) on **every** node; kube-proxy forwards `nodeIP:nodePort` to the backends. It's the simplest way to reach a Service from outside the cluster.

**Gotcha:** a nodePort outside 30000–32767 is rejected unless the apiserver's `--service-node-port-range` was widened.
questions.prompt:
Create a `NodePort` Service named `web-np` in `cni-learn` selecting `app=web`, service port `80`, pinned to nodePort `30080`.

Target: Service `web-np` is type NodePort with port 80, nodePort 30080, selector `app=web`, and endpoint addresses.
questions.hint: Write YAML with `type: NodePort` and `ports: [{port: 80, targetPort: 80, nodePort: 30080}]`, selector `app=web`. (`kubectl expose` won't let you pin the nodePort.)
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: web-np, namespace: cni-learn }
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector: { app: web }
  ports: [ { port: 80, targetPort: 80, nodePort: 30080 } ]
YAML
kubectl get svc web-np -n cni-learn

verification.description: web-np: NodePort, port 80, nodePort 30080, selector app=web, has endpoints

questions.eli5:
A ClusterIP Service is like an **internal office phone** — great, but only people inside the building can dial it. What if someone from outside needs to reach your app?

A **NodePort** Service opens a **public door on every single building (node)** in the cluster, all on the same door number. Knock on `anyNodeIP:30080` and you're let in — kube-proxy then forwards you to one of the real backend pods, no matter which node you knocked on. Even if you knock on a node that isn't running the app, it still routes you to a node that is.

NodePort doesn't replace ClusterIP — it **builds on top of it**. A NodePort Service still gets a clusterIP for internal callers; it just *also* opens the external door. It's the simplest way to reach a Service from outside the cluster without a cloud load balancer.

The door number comes from a fixed range: **30000–32767**. You can let Kubernetes pick one, or pin a specific one like `30080`.

**Watch out for:**

- **Out-of-range nodePort is rejected.** Anything outside 30000–32767 fails unless the apiserver was started with a widened `--service-node-port-range`. Don't try `80` or `8080`.
- `kubectl expose` **won't let you pin** the nodePort — write YAML (or edit after) to set `nodePort: 30080`.
- The **same port opens on every node**, even nodes with no matching pod. That's normal; traffic gets forwarded on.
- There are three ports in play and they're easy to mix up: `nodePort` (outside door), `port` (the Service's internal clusterIP port), and `targetPort` (the pod's actual port).
- Still needs a matching **selector** and **Ready endpoints** — no endpoints means the door opens onto an empty room (connection refused).
questions.deepDive:
## NodePort Services — full rundown

### The one-sentence model
A **NodePort** Service is a ClusterIP Service that **also opens the same port on every node** (default range **30000–32767**). Traffic to `anyNodeIP:nodePort` is forwarded by kube-proxy to a backend pod — the simplest way to reach a Service from outside the cluster.

### How the three port fields relate
| Field | Lives on | Who dials it | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `nodePort` | every node's IP | external clients | auto 30000–32767 |
| `port` | the Service clusterIP | in-cluster clients | required |
| `targetPort` | the pod/container | kube-proxy forwards here | = `port` |

Flow: `nodeIP:nodePort` → `clusterIP:port` → `podIP:targetPort`.

### Creating a NodePort Service
`kubectl expose` can set the type but **cannot pin** the nodePort, so use YAML to fix `30080`:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-np
  namespace: cni-learn
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
  - port: 80           # clusterIP port
    targetPort: 80     # pod port
    nodePort: 30080    # external port on every node (30000–32767)
```
Auto-assigned nodePort (don't care which):
```bash
kubectl expose deployment web --name=web-np --type=NodePort --port=80
kubectl get svc web-np               # see the assigned 3xxxx port
```

### The NodePort range
- Default: **30000–32767** (2768 ports).
- Controlled by the apiserver flag `--service-node-port-range` (e.g. `--service-node-port-range=30000-40000`).
- A pinned `nodePort` **outside the active range is rejected** at create time with a validation error.
- Pinning a port already in use by another Service → conflict error.

### externalTrafficPolicy
| Value | Behaviour | Source IP | Extra hop? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Cluster` (default) | forward to any pod cluster-wide | **SNAT'd** (client IP lost) | maybe |
| `Local` | only to pods on the node that received the packet | **preserved** | no |

With `Local`, nodes without a local backend pod **drop** the traffic (used by LBs + health checks to preserve client IP).

### Reaching it
```bash
# from outside: any node IP + the nodePort
curl http://<nodeIP>:30080
# in kind, node IPs are the docker container IPs:
docker inspect -f '{{range .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{.IPAddress}}{{end}}' <node>
# internal clients still use the clusterIP / DNS name on port 80
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Pinned nodePort must be 30000–32767** (unless the range was widened). `80`/`8080` are rejected.
- `kubectl expose` **won't pin** the nodePort — write/patch YAML for a specific port.
- The port opens on **every node**, including those without a matching pod (default `Cluster` policy forwards onward).
- Default policy **SNATs** the source IP — apps that log client IPs see the node IP unless you use `externalTrafficPolicy: Local`.
- Still needs a **matching selector + Ready endpoints**; otherwise the open port returns connection refused.
- NodePort builds on ClusterIP — the clusterIP still exists and is still the right target for in-cluster traffic.

### Quick reference
```yaml
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector: { app: web }
  ports: [ { port: 80, targetPort: 80, nodePort: 30080 } ]
```
